utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please convey to her our best wishes for a speedy recovery. From the Prosecution side, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Witness is present in the courtroom. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence. Before you do so, you need to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand you the solemn declaration, the text of the solemn declaration. Please stand up, read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. I just want to know from you whether this arrangement is to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then during your testimony we will be going into private session and I trust this has also been explained to you and all this is to guarantee your anonymity. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Witness. Good morning, counsel. I would just ask if I could have the pseudonym sheet please shown to the witness. That's identified for the record as P02462.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, please have a look at that document and let us know if that's your name that appears on it. Don't read it out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to put some questions to you initially, and I just want to remind you, in case I haven't already, that when -- when I refer to the location where you worked, I will refer to it as the southern location, and I will try to refrain from mentioning any names or locations, as I hope you will be able to do as well. First, let me start by putting this to you: Do you recall having given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor which you signed and acknowledged on the 27th of February of this year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the statement, at the time that you gave it, was that a truthful statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read your statement before coming here to testify today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you read the statement in your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that the language in which you originally gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for the purposes of the record, can you just tell us what language that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that the statement accurately reflects what you said and does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to testify -- were you to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At this time I would move to have the statement admitted, pursuant to 92 ter. That's P02463, for the record. I do have a 92 ter statement -- summary. If I can proceed with that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I need to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because Mr. Bourgon has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Just a quick -- Mr. President, along with the statement that is being offered now into evidence, under Rule 92 ter, there is an attachment which is something that does not come from this witness, which is a date book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- which he consulted, which comes from a previous witness. And this date book, or the two pages therefrom, have never been introduced in evidence before. And therefore, I do not think that this should accompany the statement and then form part of his statement. This is a separate document that has to be introduced the proper way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still we need -- we need to be able to read his statement intelligently and understand it. If it makes reference to the -- but anyway, you find -- your point is made. I mean I am not contesting that; anyway, you are correct. On the other hand, if reference it made to this page from that guy's personal date book, we would need to have it. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I -- I think we need -- I agree that we need to be able to take into account of all the documents submitted to the witness to understand his statement and apparently there were some documents that were submitted to the witness that are not annexed or attached to this statement and that have never been communicated to the Defence. I just wanted to state that for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, Madam Fauveau, if you would be kind enough to indicate precisely which documents you are referring to, we can pool all the documents together and Mr. Vanderpuye will find a way of introducing them, if he so wishes. utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to paragraph 8 of the witness's statement. It is a document that has the ERN number 03206608 to 03206637. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to address this once it has been raised. Thank you, Madam Fauveau, and thank you, Mr. Bourgon. You need to address these issues as you go along, if you are going to make use of -- but obviously you are because you are tendering the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's -- that's true. What is identified in the statement as an ERN range. My understanding is that those documents are available on the EDS. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm beginning to feel that this is one instance where it's becoming counter-productive to have the 65 ter -- 92 ter, sorry, procedure. We are going to lose more time --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I can proceed and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I -- I -- I have difficulty with my colleague proceeding under 92 ter if the statement cannot be admitted. This statement refers to documents, those documents have to come in, but those documents were never put on the Rule 65 ter list and some of these documents have never been communicated to the Defence. So we have difficulty. This was -- the preparation of this witness has been the object of two previous motions, one for the intercept itself, one to have the witness transferred and have him testify under 92 ter. Both have been the object of objections raised by the Defence, the Trial Chamber has overruled these objections, and said that the witness would come and testify. Now we find ourselves, the morning of the testimony of the witness, and we're not ready to proceed. I don't think this is fair to proceed without having all the documents and whether my colleague can tell us how he intends to introduce these documents in evidence this morning. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The matter of converting the witness to 92 ter has already been decided so it is not open for discussion. There is always the option for the Prosecution to withdraw from that position, and offer his testimony viva voce if they so desire and of course it will be open for discussion after that, but otherwise let's proceed and as we go along we see whether these problems that you are envisaging, Mr. Bourgon, materialise or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, sorry to come back to you again on this issue. In relation to the personal date book, sheet from the person's date book that is attached to the witness's statement that you referred to before, what is precisely your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The -- this morning I consulted with my colleague because that date book, for some reason I do not have it. I am consulting my colleague in the back and she does not appear to have it. It is yet to be confirmed because when I spoke to my colleague this morning, I was shown a statement with this date book attached but I have not received this so I don't know if my other colleagues from the Defence have received this date book or not, but I have not seen it yet. I just saw it this morning when I went to see my colleague. So that's where my objection comes from. How can we proceed, because this date book is the only way this witness can remember he was ever on duty during that time-frame. So it is a document that is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that, not having seen it, is because you don't have it or it's simply because when you became aware of it, it was at the end of the day, sort of and you haven't had time to see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At the moment I do not have it. I am checking with my case manager, we are taking with the other people, the other teams, and it appears that we don't have this document communicated to us this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine. Okay. But you are not in a position to say whether therefore whether this is a 65 ter document. Could we have the reference, Mr. Vanderpuye, of the personal date book of the entire document so that we can follow better?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I was preparing the witness, I imagine because this is a document that comes from a previous witness, I don't want to say the name, but it comes from a previous witness who has testified before this Trial Chamber, I imagine that this was a document in evidence in and the first thing I did coming in this morning, I checked to see what is the number of that document. Now, that's when I went to see my colleague, the document has not been entered, admitted into evidence with this previous witness, and I don't have the document yet with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Valid point. Mr. Vanderpuye, if you could help the Trial Chamber and the Defence teams by a clear indication to the reference of this personal date book from which that page is extracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's a personal date book of the -- of one of the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reference number. If it has a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It does not have a 65 ter number. It was a -- it was a page that was shown to the witness in relation to his recollection of the events concerning the date of the intercept. It's not a document that we had or in our possession, and, in fact -- and, in fact, the witness will testify as to exactly how it is he came into possession of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. You have the ERN number which is 06066236. If you could correlate that to the 65 ter number, we'll cut this discussion short. You will be able to find it. I can't help you more, Mr. Bourgon. Because I myself don't know the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There is no 65 ter number, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no 65 ter number. There is an ERN number because that document was MIFed together with the statement to make sure that the Defence counsel got it. My understanding is it's actually attached to the signed copy of the statement as part of the same ERN range. And so the ERN range of the signed document goes from 06066231 through 06066236, the last page being the document that Mr. Bourgon says he doesn't have. Now my understanding was that that document, with the ERN number on it and range, was furnished to the Defence, is in the possession of the Defence, and therefore should contain the page that's at issue. I don't know if the Court has it. But that's what it would appear, if you -- if you enter that ERN number. In addition, the statement itself refers to a range of documents that are identified by the ERN as well and the Defence obviously are in possession of that also. They certainly have access to get it, to the extent it's referenced in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move and then we see how far we can get. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we, Mr. President, say when this document, the final statement with this attachment would have been sent to the Defence, because it appears that none of my colleagues have received this statement with this attachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe that that would have been sent on or about the day that the document was signed, which would have been on the 27th of February. That was the day that the document was -- was assigned an ERN number, as it were, or MIFed, I think is the term. I had in advance of this statement, sent the Defence a copy of the unsigned version of the statement because I didn't have the ability obviously to process the signed document, indicated in an e-mail that the statement I was sending was unsigned and, in fact, that the witness had signed the statement and that would be forthcoming. And in the statement it refers to the documents that are -- in the statement that I sent that was unsigned obviously refers to the documents that are at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I -- looking at the -- on the e-court system, this document that my colleague is referring to has been uploaded on the e-court system under Prosecution documents. We can just see it now on the e-court. But it appears that it wasn't sent to us, and we never got any -- that the copy of the final statement or of the attachment that came along with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to check, Mr. Bourgon. It seems that this document was put on e-court on the 28th of February, and on the same day or thereabouts, you received, in relation to this witness, the list of documents that the Prosecution intended to make use of, and that this particular page was amongst the documents indicated by the Prosecution. In any case, because I mean we try to be as practical as possible, if you wish -- if you are not in a position to cross-examine the witness in relation to this document immediately, perhaps we can put you last in the list, and cross-examine him when you have had time to refer to this page and after maybe having heard his testimony as well as the cross-examination of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have -- I will be able to proceed. I will get a copy and we have it on screen now. And I will be able to proceed. However, I -- I do have the list of exhibit that you are referring to under 92 ter for Witness 186 and it does refer to document 2463, which is the witness statement dated 26 February under seal. Now, I have yet to check if this includes that document or not, but I will be able to proceed this morning. But I maintain, nonetheless, my objection that this is a document that is now being provided to the Court and that has not been either on the Rule 65 ter list and that has not been either -- there has never been any request for this document to be used, whereas the litigation concerning this witness and this particular intercept, dated January of 1995, months before the events that we are talking about, this litigation has been going for a lot of time, and still we do not have a request by the Prosecution to have this document admitted, not admitted, but included on its Rule 65 ter list. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to prolong this discussion much further, but in the Prosecution exhibit list in -- circulated on the 28th, the second document, that's the one after the pseudonym sheet, is the OTP's witness statement dated 26th February, which would be 27th, and the pages indicated run from 06066231, which would be the first page of the cover sheet of the statement, right to and inclusive of the page which is -- look at me, which is the extract or extract from the book. This is included as part of the documents that the Prosecution wish to tender with this witness. So to me it means that this is being included by them in the statement itself as part of the statement. But let's proceed. Because I think the further we prolong it, the more complicated it becomes. Mr. Vanderpuye. Sorry you have had to sit down and listen to -- but perhaps other witnesses or other persons will understand that sometimes you are kept waiting in the room because we have got procedural problems to deal with and they are always time consuming. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do have this 92 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like to go into private session just, I think, for the first couple of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thereafter, the witness was assigned to the northern site until his demobilisation in April of 1996. As a commander at the southern site, the witness described the procedure applied to the interception process which includes the following: The monitoring of radio channels, the recording of conversations, the transcription of these conversations on to paper or notebooks, and the typing and sending of information in an encrypted form. The witness personally typed and sent such reports. The witness reviewed entries from the date book of a fellow commander of the second detachment assigned to the southern site which indicated that this second detachment worked through January 16th, 1995 and then resumed work on January 26, 1995. During the intervening period, the witness's detachment was on duty. The witness reviewed a report dated 19 January, 1995, detailing the condition of the equipment located at the southern site and bearing his name as the sender of the report. The witness confirmed that he typed and sent out such equipment status reports regularly and that he sent the report dated 19 January, 1995. The witness further reviewed a report containing an intercept recorded at 10.57 hours on 19 January, 1995. The witness confirmed that the intercept was processed by his unit and that such reports were regularly typed and sent by him daily to the automatic data processing unit. That concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do have a few questions I would like to put to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, as a commander of the unit in which you worked, can you tell us relatively briefly what your responsibilities were with respect to the training, supervision, for example, of your men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. When people were transferred from the OG 3 to the 2nd Corps I trained my subordinates, I trained them to work on radio equipment for scanning frequencies and interception of radio relay conversations. This training mostly boiled down to the familiarisation with the equipment and the method of work switching on the equipment, transfer of audio recording on to the paper, and then the procedure would proceed through me. In other words, they had to be familiar with the equipment. This is as far as the training of my men went. My other tasks were this: Every morning and during the day, if there was no activity on the radio relay routes that we followed, I would scan the band from 230 to 270 megahertz for RR1 and from 610 to 980 in order to maybe observe some new active frequency. My following task was to control and perform minor repairs of the radio equipment, antennas and cables. And the last part was work on PC or as a radio operator, I was familiar with work on PC typing and automatic data processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you have responsibility for maintaining the schedules with respect to the men that you supervised, administrative tasks such as that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. These were my tasks, my regular tasks as a commander deploying people, working out shifts, sometimes shifts had to be prolonged or curtailed. It all depended on the activity and the quantity of information we collected and dispatched. In order to have a good concentration of people working on equipment, sometimes we had to curtail information in order to help the radio operator to be concentrated enough to be able to monitor conversations on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the transcription of intercepts itself, were your men permitted to draw inferences from the information they received, to assume things or to guess?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No, no. Your Honours, it is my duty to provide a short explanation at this point. In the -- in the profession that deals with the interception of radio relay conversation, conversations, information is only useful and of good quality if it is credibility and if it is timely and if it dispatched for the automatic data processing in time. If the radio operator does not understand a word or is not sure of the accuracy of the word, then he had to ask one or two colleagues of his to listen to the conversation again, and if the three of them did not understand the word, we would put in slash brackets intelligible [as interpreted] because if you speculated and you didn't understand the word, it could lead people in the automatic data processing astray. I claim that nobody was allowed to add or speculate. If they didn't understand, they would have to indicate that in brackets by putting words intelligible [as interpreted] or "I don't understand." Something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during your tenure as a commander, did you give them that specific instruction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: As for the specific instruction, this is something that people adopted in the first part. As soon as they moved to the 2nd Corps, they already were familiar with the technique, they were familiar with the modulations of things that they were listening to. And then I would try to explain the technical aspects of the equipment. Since I had worked in the JNA for a while, I was familiar with radio relay communication system, and then I would tell them that what they were learning was not only mechanical process, that they had to understand why things were why they were, why there was signal, why there was no modulation. I was there all the time. I was providing them advice. I didn't have very specific working hours. I would supervise them all the time. Sometimes I would provide them with more detailed information and I would make sure that they understood the technicalities of what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the intercepts that had been transcribed, was it the responsibility of the unit to send this information to another unit in a timely fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was it the responsibility of the person sending that information to extract the information from the handwritten material accurately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If there were omissions in typing handwritten material by a PC and we did that in the editor, if there was an omission or a mistake, then -- then this transcript would not be credible. This was taken into account because, I repeat, if there was a typo or an omission in transcribing the audio recordings, then this might have led people in the automatic data processing astray and they would not have been able to do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, in January of 1995, who was responsible for typing and sending the intercepted material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: All the time that I spent in the 2nd Corps in the -- in this unit, I was the only one in that department that I was a member of who was working on the PC and who was sending dispatches to the automatic data processing department.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was anybody besides you during that period of time -- well, was anybody besides you during that period of time authorised to use the computer or otherwise have access to the computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the material that you sent and typed, did you maintain a file of these electronic transmissions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Whatever was sent can be found in the SP 610 programme, and this remained there as proof. The programme itself stores whatever is sent, and in the PC I had folders by the year, by the month, and by the date, and on every date there were two folders, one was for dispatches, one was for received materials. And the received materials were suggestions from the commander or similar documents. And I would open documents and store it into the folder for that day. And this was my archive of all the conversations that we dispatched for the automatic data processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question that perhaps would help us understand better. Were these stored in an encrypted form in the -- in the computer? That's number one. And secondly, was the encrypting software installed on the computer the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The archive was not encrypted. It was in the original form. And it was encrypted before it was sent through the Paket radio system. The archive form was in a normal form. And before it was sent, we would use the programme for encrypting and then it is then downloaded from the SB 610 programme as an encrypted document and as such it was sent to the automatic data processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, are you going to deal with this SB 610 programme a little bit in detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've heard the Court's question. Can you tell us a little bit about this SP 610 programme and how it relates to the Paket radio system?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. This SP 610 programme, version 610, is a programme for Paket radio system that was used by ham radio operators. It was in Windows, and some basic features of the programme were this: I had 10 channels that could be active all simultaneously, and when I was sending data using this programme, the programme user had a possibility, if the channels were overbooked or if the communication was not good, he could manually reduce the number of characters in the package that he was sending. In principle, this is 255 characters, or packets. How would this work? He would take a packet and send it to the modem at that time we used VICOM. VICOM prepared it to be understandable by the radio equipment. It takes by the microphone and through the correspondence PC comes to the end user's PC. And then this is returned to my PC. My PC receives the package and compares it to the package that has just been sent. If there is a congruence, if there is a match, then my PC confirms the accuracy of the package and starts sending a new package. In an alternative case, if the return package is not the same, is not matching the original one, then the PC confirms the irregularity of the package and starts resending the original package. And in the programme itself, there is a frame in which you can see how many times the PC, i.e., the programme, has sent this particular package or packet. In the programme itself, there is a chat mode possibility. For example, I could communicate in a written form with my correspondent. I could communicate with them and everything that is going on on that particular frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much for that. Let me just ask this so at least I have it a little clearer in my own head. Is this Paket radio system essentially a wireless, digital network?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. The data dispatch was in a digital form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it basically set up with a computer, a transceiver and a type of modem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. A computer, a modem, a radio receiver and of course an antenna.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And does it work in a way that the data that leaves the computer enters a modem and is changed to a form that can then be sent through the transceiver -- transmitter, I should say, to the antenna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the packets you are talking about here, you are talking about specific amounts of data sent from one computer to another. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: When I spoke about the quantity of characters in a packet, this is just one part of a complete, typed report. SP610 takes a packet with 255 characters or lower number of characters to speed up the communication between the two PCs and the SP PC that receives the packet, this second PC has to confirm the accuracy of the packet. It is not just one whole report, written report as one packet, but various parts of that document, each of them feature as one packet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you're referring to the data that comprises the report that makes up the report, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was it your responsibility as a commander to regularly fill out reports about the condition of the equipment located at the -- at the site where you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. That was my obligation every day. I had to report on the state of the equipment, I had to put my remarks and requirements for the upcoming period. And I also had to account for the number of men who were on leave, who were on sick leave and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, at the end of those reports did you normally type your name as the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did anybody in your unit other than you have the authority to put your name on such a document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you prepare such a report on the 19th of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that indicative of whether or not you were working on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: This indicates that on that day I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And on the days that you worked, was there anybody besides you that was responsible for sending or typing or encrypting transcripts of radio relay intercepts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document, if I could. P02437A and B. In e-court, please. All right. First I would just like to start with this page, if I could. The first thing I'd like to draw your attention to is have you seen -- I just want to make sure it's not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is not being broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first thing I want to do is refer you to the header on this document. Do you see a date that's indicated on this header?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's fair to say that that is the 19th of January, 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And there is also a location. Don't read it out, but can you confirm that that's the location that you worked at on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, there's some other information that's below that. In particular, there's an entry on this document that reads, "RM br. 1" do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell the Court what that indicates, what that shows? Or what it means, I should say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: RM number 1 is workstation number 1. In our room where we worked. This is the physical place of work, the place where the operator worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does that -- does that reference correspond to an actual location within the unit that you commanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And next to that there is an indication of "IC-100/RRU 1." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what that indicates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: This is the piece of equipment that we used to monitor the radio relay route, and RRU-1 is the mark for the radio relay equipment 1, which was the means of communication of -- of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that information consistent with the equipment that was used at your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the date, were you required to enter that information when you sent a report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you sent a report, was that sent on the same day that the transcription was actually taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. The practice was to send out the information as soon as possible to the -- to the automatic data processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one second. Okay. Could we now go to page 3 of this document, please. I need to go to the bottom of the document. That's great. Okay. If I could just refer your attention to an entry that's made on this report that is timed at 10.57. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'm sorry. And can you tell us whether or not that is an entry that is consistent with information that was captured at your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what about this entry can you tell us is consistent with it having been captured at your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: The frequency here is 785.000 so you can conclude that we were monitoring RRU-800, which is the radio relay device used by the JNA, which was 610 to 960 megahertz. Then there is this information which indicates how we manage to monitor those frequencies without having the adequate equipment. With a radio receiver, with that frequency range, we monitored 785.000 megahertz. We also had a signal at the ultrashort-wave device. There was a modulator or a mixer with a local oscillator and that frequency was modulated and was sent from that modulator to the KT device, that was the Kenwood TS-450 and then the channels were separated because the RRU-800 device can send 12 channels. It has that option. Had we not done this conversion, this modulation, and then the division at the KT, it would be as if somebody was speaking to me, 12 different voices were speaking to me in my earphones and I wouldn't be able to understand them. So then what this indicates is that we had the local device, transferred it to the KT, memorised them, and then from that device we would transfer the channels to another device. And this is how we were able to separate the channels and monitor what was actually being broadcast by the RRU device.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can I ask you, do you see a reference below the participants to "RR," and then it says "trasa Zvornik-Vlasenica." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether or not that was within the range of the areas that were monitored by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear for the record, could you just tell us what that means, the part where it says "RR trasa"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: It means the radio relay route.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you have previously seen the date at the beginning of this document. Had you been working on that date, would you have been the one to have typed this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you have any doubt about the fact that you were working on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No. I was absent only in September 1994 when I went to a training course and the New Year 1995. I had some private problems and these are my only two absences, when I was not actually on the schedule at the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you have an opportunity to review entries of a date book of a fellow commander prior to coming here to testify? Don't tell us his name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have an opportunity or look at the entries that a colleague of yours or a fellow commander had put in a personal date book prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Could I just have P02463 uploaded into the e-court for a moment. All right. If I could just refer to -- oh, the English version of it, I'm sorry. And refer to the last page, which is 0606-6236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you go into private session a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I would just ask that the document not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is not being broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Maybe we can blow it up a little bit. And I think we need to go -- I think we need to go to the bottom of the page. In any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the document that you reviewed, the date book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just so that the Court is clear, can you -- well, first of all, can you tell us, did you come into possession of this date book yourself, physically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you retrieve the date book from the colleague to whom it belongs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you bring that with you when you came to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And after having reviewed this, these entries, did that assist you in any way in determining whether or not your particular detachment was working on the 19th of January of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see that here, that they finished their shift on the 16th of January, 1995. The last shift was from 10.00 to 1400 hours. Excuse me. And then from 1400 hours our group took over. Our group came on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the other group came back on duty? And I'll ask that the document be moved over to the right and to the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: The colleague came on duty again with his group on the 26th of January, 1995. The first shift was from 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, between your colleague's group and your group, were there any other groups that worked at that particular location? With whom you alternated, I should say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No, no. It was just our two groups at that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Having reviewed the report, that is the typed version of the intercept, do you have any reason do believe that what you saw of the intercept is anything different than what was sent by your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I don't see any reason that they should be different -- there should be any differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, that concludes my direct examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to begin precisely where my colleague left off, about the notebook that you looked at. Can you please tell me, why did you look at the book? Why did you go through it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: It was my colleague's diary from the other shift, and I brought the book with me to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hand the book over to somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I handed it over on the 22nd of February. The 22nd of February -- no, no, excuse me. On the 26th of February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell me to whom you gave the book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: To the gentleman who took the statement, who took my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is he from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me how you got the idea to take the book with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: My colleague got in touch with me, and he offered it. I didn't take this document -- kind of documentation home with me or kept it with me after I was demobilised. I didn't have any need to. But this was his private document, so he offered it to me and he said maybe there will be something there that I will need. So that's how that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me, since we didn't have the opportunity to look at the notebook, is it a large notebook? Are there many pages, or is it just these two pages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I think it's a small A4 notebook. More or less A4 format, and it has several pages. It's his kind of record, the deployment of his people, staff, when he was on the shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you something else. We have different information about how information or data was entered into the computer. Amongst other things, you have seen the report that my learned friend from the Prosecution showed you where there is the heading with the date and the number under which the reports were sent. My question is, when the information was entered into the computer, does the computer programme assign this number of the report and the date, or is this entered by hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: At the time we used queue editor for data entry. Everything was entered by hand. It wasn't like this, like it is now with Windows, where it is automatic. So everything was entered by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that there is no confusion, I am only asking about the date and the number, not about the text of the report.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I'm talking about the date. The Q editor is a very simple typing programme, that's why I mentioned it. It's not like Windows Word where you can copy, paste and you can transfer the date from one file to another. For each file, when you opened it, you had to type it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are moving at a terrific speed. Please, slow down. Slow down. I wouldn't like to be in the interpreters' shoes. They are making a real big effort. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry. Excuse me for the interruption. On page 30, line 21, I thought the witness in his response said that at the time we used the Q editor for data entry, everything was entered by hand. It was not like the Windows and then he proceeds to say where it was automatic, so everything was entered by hand. I thought that's the way it was but we can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Ostojic, for pointing that out. It makes sense. Perhaps the witness can confirm that and I see him nodding. But please, Witness, and Mr. Zivanovic, you both speak your language, both highly intelligent people. And you tend to answer -- put questions in a fast mode. So please slow down and allow a pause between question and answer. I mean everything that is being said by you in your own language needs to be translated to us in English and -- and in French. So that usually takes time a little bit longer. So, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have seen the report that was shown to you by my colleague, and you explained to us that the packet that the reports are sent in, they are practically sent -- the reports are sent with a certain number of characters, so frequently an entire report does not fit into one packet that is sent but is divided into several packets. If I understood you correctly. What I would like to ask you is, when you look at this report that was shown to you, can you tell us how many packages were required to send out such a report? You can give us an approximate number if you are able to do that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: It's hard to say how many packets that is now. The fact is that in your question I didn't hear everything in its entirety. Not the whole report was packed into several packets, but the parts of the report, for example, 255 characters are picked up, they are sent off, then confirmation is received, then veracity is confirmed or not, and then a new batch of 255 characters are sent off and that's how it goes until the end of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that. So my question is, when you look at a report that you just saw before, can you please tell us whether you were able to send this off in one packet or whether this was not possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No, not in one packet. 255 characters is too little for a report like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you mean a larger number of packets?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't heed what I told you. Again you are jumping with questions and answers without even the least pause. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So in any case, this had to be sent in several packets, a report of this kind. Well, let's close this topic, if you are unable to tell us approximately how many packets would be required to send off a report like this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No, I cannot give you an approximate number. You would need to count the characters, but definitely it could not be packed into one packet, this entire report. Because -- excuse me. When you look at the report, you cannot look at it like this, it would have to be encrypted. We have spaces here, space between words, two or three spaces. When it's encrypted, the report, if you were to look at it, then it looks more like a series of hieroglyphs with no spaces in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand. Thank you. Can we move into private session now, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is going next? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of areas I would like to cover with you so I can understand this process a little better. Can you share with us -- you spoke of this SP 610 programme, and can you explain to me some of the features that that programme had in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. SP 610 programme was used for Paket radio, and I already said that ham radio operators had used it before. It features a tape with my code signal. It also features 10 channels, and I could be connected with 10 correspondents. Each of the channels, when you change the channel, there is a round band where I see the signal code of the corresponded with whom I am connected. I can use these to change the channel and then I also have a chat mode through which we can monitor what we call traffic. I can monitor traffic, and in the central window of the monitor, we can chat like we do today on the Internet. We receive information through this so-called chat mode. If there is anything else you wish me to tell you about the software, I can tell you. In other words, I use a modem, this was a VICOM model which contains two integrals since 7041 was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. Did the programme have a lock key or a key-lock mechanism to capture the data that you were actually typing in, and that no one can then edit that data? Did it have that type of mechanism?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: The mechanism as such did not exist. Maybe I should try and explain this. I apologise. I don't mean to offend anybody. Your profession, you use words in order to prove things, and we technicians, we do it by our hands. When I type a file, when I type a report in the editor programme, then I process it in the programme or software for encrypting. When I can -- want to connect with the correspond, I call for the encrypted file, and then I send it, all the files in their original forms, the typed forms will remain in the folder system under the year, the month and the date. SP 610 programme sends the encrypted report immediately to the correspondent. I did not have a special mechanism to store the encrypted material. I could only store the original typed forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I would like to focus on. The original typed forms that remained in the folder system, when you said under the date, month or year, that you captured certain conversations, were you able, subsequent to that, was there a capability, and I'm not suggesting that you did this, sir, but was there a capability to edit those folders, as you call them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: There was a technical capability. However, when I type a file, I send it immediately to the data processing unit. And what was left in my archives I processed myself in order to make some conclusions. To help myself, I would create my own network in order to be able to compare some things. But the report, by then, has already been sent to the automatic data processing. I did not see the purpose or the goal of anybody to fiddle with the report. Because I've already told you the information that we sent had to be sent in a timely fashion and it had to be reliable, it had to be credible, and this all depended on the speed at which it was dispatched.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, don't -- I'm asking you this respectfully. Please don't read into my questions. I'm not suggesting that you went back and edited it, but you were one of the commanders of the northern site in 1995, correct? I meant to say southern site, but I said northern. Southern site, if I may correct that. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when we say 1995, I know we talked about intercept in January 1995, you were also the commander of that same southern site in July of 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. Up to the moment when I was demobilised I was the commander of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think you gave us that date as 1996, but we'll leave as the record. Let me ask you, the same process that you explained during your direct and that was read in your 92 ter statement, did you utilise that statement process in January as you would have in July of 1995? Meaning the same way, you were the only one who was the typist? Is that the way it worked in July as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. You said 1996, I believe it was in the -- in April, on the 5th of April, 1996 when I was demobilised. And up to then I did what I did. But the whole unit was transferred to a different location at one point. I continued typing for my own department, and I believe that this was in November 1995 when we were relocated. The same unit, the same people, the same equipment, relocated to another location, but I continued performing the same tasks for my own department as of then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that's the information we have, November 1995, and then you were ultimately demobilised in April of 1996. I'm not concerned about that so much, what I'm concerned about specifically and you may have answered it, but I want to clarify it for the record. In July of 1995, were you the only one who would actually enter or type this information as you've described it, in the computer, while using the SP 610 programme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, as the commander of the southern site in July of 1995, can you tell me when the Prosecutor first contacted you to discuss your role with the intercepts or what we've called the intercept project? When were you first contacted to assist and give evidence to this Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: On the 20th -- no, before that. I was contacted by phone. On the 22nd of February, I believe that this was when I had my first contact on the issues of intercept -- on the issue of intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And help me with this: Not 1996, but actually 2007, correct? That's when they first contacted you, correct? 2007. I know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm sorry. Yes, yes. On the 22nd of February 2007 we had our telephone contact on the issue of intercepted conversations. A gentleman from -- I believe he was an investigator, he had contacted me before in order to see whether I would be willing to testify, whether I still remembered certain things. But he didn't mention anything specific about any conversation. This was just an introduction to any future contacts that I would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Now, did you first get contacted by this investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor or did you have this conversation with your friend, and please don't mention his name, who shared with you his diary, I think, as we've called it? Do you know what I'm talking about, which friend and which diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: After my initial introductory contact, and before I left to come here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you look through the entire book to see if, in fact, January -- strike that. If, in fact, July 1995 and the work schedule was identified in that diary of this friend of yours that you brought to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I would not be honest if I told you that I looked at every single page. But I did look at had this particular part that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to July -- January -- I'm referring, sir, to July of 1995. Did you look at the work schedule for July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I don't think that I did not look -- I didn't look at July, I -- I mostly dwelled upon January 1995. I didn't pay so much attention to other dates, I focused on January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well I had an opportunity for about three minutes to look at that logbook, and I tried to scan through to find July 1995, and it -- if we could be kind enough, with the Court's permission and the assistance of the usher, to have the-- give the original diary book to the witness, I have a couple of concrete questions on that. If you don't mind, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have it available, yes. Do you need to refer him to any particular page or...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not numbered, but I think I could direct him to it, I think. If not, I can get it and then give it back to him, if that's okay with --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you find the approximate page where it starts with May 1995. Could you maybe look through that logbook for me. I said May, specifically for a reason, but maybe you could help us. It's in the middle of the logbook or diary. Or if they give it to me, I could just direct them right to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that would be easier, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just keep going. Thank you. I apologise. Your Honour, we can maybe place it on the ELMO but then we should not broadcast because it obviously identifies the various operators on certain pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may ask him this question so he can orientate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This seems to be about the middle of the book, correct, Mr. Witness? The middle of the diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Somewhat after the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, fair enough. On the left-hand side we see that -- can you tell us what date this entry is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I don't think I can say it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I see what seems to be with the red ink 26-05 but I'm not asking you to confirm that. Do you see following that, sir, that there were several pages that were pulled out of the original diary? Do you see that if you look at the original, can you make that -- do you have that understanding as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if you look, there is one page that's left with almost a quarter inch of the page, but then after that there seems to be an additional several pages, maybe five to 10 pages that were torn out of the book. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ask your friend why there were pages missing from this diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why someone would want to pull out pages out of this diary specifically apparently a period after, I contend, after the 26th of May, why they would tear out those pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to the question. It seems to me that it calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think -- I think it's a fair question. If he knows the answer, he will give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It also assumed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he doesn't, he's not to speculate. He knows that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It also assumes a fact that is not in evidence which is whether or not it was actually torn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The alternative is pages have fallen out of the -- and got lost, deliberately got lost. So let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have to answer to this because I -- the witness said yes to my question that they were torn out, but in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you want me to restate the question, if the Court permits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We don't want you to speculate. I want to know if you know. Do you have any idea why someone would want to pull out pages out of this diary specifically for the period following the 26th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I don't know. If the diary were mine, then I might be able to remember or explain why the pages were pulled out. Since this was not my diary, I can only speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you for that, and thank you for helping us at least clarify that issue with respect to the diary. I want to change the subject so I do not need the diary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, can I know what date it is that's appearing after this torn out page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can take a look. I didn't actually go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like to see. You can see, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's blank pages, Your Honour. But I didn't go through each one, but we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I leave it to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll follow up. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we see what the next date is or the next entry in this diary. Can you find it for us, sir. If you don't mind, quickly, or however you'd like to do it, if you could find the next entry in the diary. Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: The following entry is an electronic scheme of a pre-amplifier, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think, although I had a cursory review of the diary, that the balance of the diary book, meaning up to -- starting from this scheme, after that date that I contend is the 26th of May, 1995, there are other schematics or other drawings in connection with the various equipment that may or may not have been used, correct? The rest of the pages, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Can I have a look at the following pages, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I see are schemes. Ham operators always do that. We collect schemes. These are all filters, BW 52, this is another pre-amplifier. This is the scheme of a pre-amplifier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, going back to this SP 610, and this computer system and the folders that you would send out in the encrypted version. Did you retain a copy of those folders with the typed version of the conversations in your computer that you could personally maintain or what did you do with that after you were demobilised or after you left the southern site in November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I apologise, SP 610 is software, it is not a piece of equipment. Up to the moment when I was demobilised, we kept this in our archives and we retained it in PC and once I was demobilised, obviously, this wasn't my personal equipment, I couldn't take anything home, everything was left with the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand that it is software, sir, but it is maintained in the hard drive of the computer, is it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: The archives, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, sir, is did you turn that equipment in which had the software which contained the folders, did you turn it over to anyone in specific, given that you were commander of the southern site, any time after -- any time during November 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Look here, what I am given as my basic equipment -- obviously I could not be demobilised if I had not returned all those. Only when I returned all the equipment, I could be demobilised, and all that equipment, everything that I had worked on, remained with the unit. I don't know what came of it after I was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm not suggesting anything, and I understand the process. My question is, if we still have this equipment, this computer that may or may not have been retrieved from the southern site, would the material or the folders, as you call them, still be in the computer, saved in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the witness has already answered the question. And he's -- he's said that he doesn't know what happened to it once he left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It might be a slightly different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In a way you have already answered this question which was put in a different manner before. However, if you would like to add anything, particularly addressing this particular question that has now been put to you, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there is anything else to add, as the gentleman has said this remains in the hard drive. It's normal. I don't know what happened to the files later on. There might have been a virus that entered the hard drive, but this would only be my speculation. What I said stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So on the day you left the site and the unit, to your knowledge, this material was still there stored in the computer. Is that -- would that be a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, everything was stored in the folders and all this had to remain in the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge at all as to what happened to that material stored in that computer after you left? Did you receive any news or any information which could enlighten us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to go to another topic related. But I'd, with the Court's permission, to go into private session just to identify a name that was used before?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into previous session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This individual that we just talked about, how often did you see him in June and July of 1995, whereupon he took the archives to the 2nd Corps? Was it daily, weekly, monthly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Look, when I was talking about this gentleman whose name I'm not going to mention again, I didn't say that he was there on that day. And as far as I can remember, the question was not about either that particular day or that particular month. It was just put to me to explain the procedure, and to say what happened to the material and as to your specific question, I can tell you that I saw him during our hand-overs, the change of shifts. And they -- those hand-over of shifts were not the same in the summer and in the winter. For example in the winter, if there was a lot of snow, people would stay on shift for longer time. In the summer this time would be shorter. Sometimes he would come to make rounds, to inspect. Sometimes it would be every day, sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not so interested in the period when it was snowing. What about in the summertime? Do you recall in June and July of 1995 whether this gentleman would come on a daily basis to your southern site to pick up materials in order to archive them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No, not every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Give me an approximation so we can have a better understanding how often, to the best of your recollection, did he come to retrieve these materials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: He would be present at every change of shift. But if there were a number of audio recordings and if we were faced with a situation that we would have to start working on the reserve tapes then we would communicate with them and they would come, collect the full tapes and they would bring us new, fresh tapes so that we always had tapes in reserve. Sometimes, if they assessed that they needed to talk to us or take a particular tape which was important in their view, they would come and collect it on the same day. So they would not come to collect the typed conversations but the original tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you. I may have misunderstood when you said shift, and you mean shift by whatever that 10 or 12 or 15-day period that your unit was assigned the tasks that you have described earlier, correct? So he would come at the end of your shift, meaning those X amount of days, I think it was 15 or so, that you worked, correct? With the exceptions that you have listed here for us now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: The shift actually meant the hand-over of duty. When one shift was being relieved by another shift. That was what I meant. The changeover. And I emphasise that one of them would be there definitely but there were also cases when they would come for an inspection. These would be my superior officers who would come for an inspection. It could be every five days or a week, and these spot checks were not something that was announced in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with those kind of supervisors. But in any event, can you tell us, sir, because in the area of the military that you worked, in that southern site, was there ever a logbook that would record who would be entering and exiting the southern site? Do you ever maintain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: From what I can remember, at the time, no, because we had security at that location. So all the security matters in relation to the actual facility was something that was in their jurisdiction. They were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was the name of the unit that was providing that security that had the jurisdiction to permit people to enter or exit the southern site in July of 1995? And if you need to go into private session, we can, but I don't know that it's necessarily necessary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I think it was called -- the unit, it was a 2nd Corps unit, it was called the unit for security of facilities and persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, going back to this gentleman who was the one retrieving or taking the archives from the southern site, while you were the commander there, did he ever give you a receipt or a document identifying what materials he was taking out of the southern site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there was ever a policy or procedure to have any time you transfer archived material or documents of that sort, to record anywhere what was being given to this individual or any other individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I don't remember that such records were kept. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I need to begin my cross-examination to go back to an issue which was raised by both of my Defence colleagues in order to get further clarification. I refer back to page 40, lines 5 to 6 of the transcript, and that is for the benefit of my colleague. You mentioned that the moment at which you contacted your friend to get the diary, or about the diary, was after the first contact with the investigator, and before leaving for The Hague. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to know is -- my understanding is that there was a second phone interview with the investigator before you came to The Hague. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: On the 22nd of February, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this would be the second contact, at which point you answered questions to the investigator. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: It was mostly about my personal information, that's what we talked about. My particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I'd like to know, Witness, is whose idea was it in the first place to consult the diary which belongs to your friend? Was that suggested to you by the investigator or did you come up with the idea?
