For example, I will contact my friend, this way maybe I can sort out whether I was on duty or not on the 19th of January. How did it all come about? Whose idea was it at first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: In the first conversation I wasn't able to confirm definitely whether I was at the facility then, meaning at specific dates. However, recalling what New Years eve I spent at the facility and which one at home, then I kind of felt that I may have been up there in January. I wasn't able to state the exact dates. And perhaps the colleague also had some sort of documentation. Do you understand? Because at that moment I wasn't able to recall that, yes, on such-and-such date I was there. My memory isn't as good at that. But recalling the New Years eve and some other things, I knew that I was definitely there in January. And my colleague got in touch with me by telephone and said that he had some documents. If I remember correctly, perhaps the investigator asked me if the colleague could have anything, but in any case, I really cannot say. You know, maybe he did have something like a document, something in his home archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, I fully understand that January of 1995 is a very long time ago, and it is not possible for you to recall everything during that period. However, what I have difficulty understanding is that you are having a conversation with or a telephone interview with an investigator, you cannot recall, you have an idea that you might have been there in January but you can't recall exactly if you are. But then your colleague gives you a call. How did your colleague know that you were into that conversation with that investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I didn't have an idea that perhaps I was there; I knew I was there for sure. But it was just a matter of dates. As for whether someone else contacted my colleague, I really didn't discuss that with him. He simply gave this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I take it, Witness, that you met with your colleague to -- so that he could hand over this diary to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did your friend inform you that he had testified before this Tribunal in the same case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: When he gave me the diary, it was a very brief meeting, and we didn't discuss that, but from earlier knowledge, I know that he did testify with protective measures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did your friend ever discuss with you the contents of his testimony, not so much the exact contents, but how this thing -- how testifying before the International Tribunal works? Did he share that with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And my last question on this topic, with regards to the diary, did your friend inform you or provide you with any information concerning the diary? And I refer now to the questions which were posed to you by my colleague concerning the fact that pages were missing or which period it covered.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did your friend mention to you whether he had shown this diary when he testified or whether he had given it to the investigators of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: He didn't tell me that. As to whether he did give it or not, I really don't know. But he himself didn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, the diary, I think you still have it with you. And from what I could see when I looked at it during the break, there are a series of pages that are kind of detached that are at the end of the diary. Did your colleague provide you any information with these pages or any guidance, make sure you don't lose them, this is counted? Did he tell you anything about the diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move on to another topic. And I'd like to -- you to confirm that the conversation which was shown to you this morning, I'm talking about the intercept, that you yourself were not -- you were not the one who listened or who heard that conversation and who transcribed it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I was not the one who recorded the conversation, and who then transcribed by using headphones, the audio recording to paper. This is not something that I did. I was not doing radio surveillance. The person who is monitoring the equipment with headphones, that is not something that was my job. I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you assist the Trial Chamber today by telling us which of the operators did the actual listening and transcribing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I -- I think I know what you're going to say. If he -- if you are requesting him to mention a name, we need to go into private session. All right? Is that what you had in mind, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is one of the things I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The other is for -- if my colleague could be more specific with respect to what period he's talking about or what intercept he's talking about, because the question seems like it could call for a whole list of the roster of operators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure you are correct. I think all along I was thinking he was referring to this particular, but correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We're talking about the same intercept, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I think maybe that might be a good opportunity to mention that when the Prosecution applied to have this witness testify here, we were informed and the Trial Chamber was informed, that he was about to testify about several intercepts. But there is only one, and that's only the one I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me make that question more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You still haven't told us whether we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not necessary, because I will change the way I ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you know the identity of the exact operator who listened to the conversation and who transcribed it? Do you know who it is exactly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Without mentioning the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Without mentioning the name, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot say who it was. It's been a long time since then and I really don't know whether X, Y or Z transcribed a specific conversation. It's been too long. I can say one of those people, but it's not possible to say such-and-such person transcribed it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That's what I suspected. That's why we don't need to get into names. But can you also confirm that this conversation in or on specifically 19 January, 1995, that if you are the one who -- who typed the conversation, that it was given to you on a piece of paper, because notebooks were not available at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: It's correct that it was I who typed it from the paper into the computer. But I really cannot say definitely whether it was typed from a piece of paper or from a notebook. That is something that I really cannot do. We used a lot of old archives, papers that were typed on with a typewriter on one side, and then we turned them over and used the blank side to transcribe conversations. So I cannot remember whether it was a piece of paper or a notebook, but I was the one who would type such data from the paper or the notebook into the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you remember whether notebooks were available in January of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to that specific intercept, we're always talking about the same one, my understanding is that you were not shown the -- the handwritten version of this conversation because it is not available today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Well, I did have it then when I was typing it, and I hope nobody interprets this the wrong way now, no. At that time, yes, I had to have it in order to type it into the computer, but at this time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was the purpose of my question, at this time. Now, my colleague asked you a question, and I refer here to page 22, lines 3 to 4 of the transcript, and the question was as follows: "Did you file a report concerning the status of the equipment on 19 January?" And your answer was "Yes." Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, and I think that I also said that such regular reports about the state of the equipment, whether it was operational or not, was something that was sent out every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question concerning this specific report of 19 January, that's the question which was posed to you, I suggest that, unless I show you specifically this report today, that you could not remember that on 19th of January you filed such a report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will. In response to a question by my colleague, you mentioned that you filed a report on the status of the equipment on 19th January, 1995. My question is, without seeing such a report with your name on it, you could not tell the Court today that you indeed filed a report on that date. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes. The report that would have a date with my signature, then of course I was the one who sent it. To be honest, if it wasn't for that, and if I didn't have the notebook from my colleague, I really wouldn't be able to remember. If you were to ask me now, for example, about October 1994, it would be very difficult to say if I was there definitely on a specific date without having some kind of aide such as a dispatch by me or the schedule of shifts, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would like now if we could have on e-court, both the English version and the B/C/S version, of 2437, that is Alpha in English and B for Bravo in B/C/S. If we can have this in e-court, please.

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't really think it's necessary, but really it's up to the witness whether he feels that this information could allow someone to identify him. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. President, is he has been identified as the commander of that unit and there weren't that many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we don't even need to refer -- refer the matter to the witness. Let's redact lines 4 to 8, please, of this page, page 58. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. And thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I should have been more careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we can on the e-court both the Alpha and Bravo side by side, please. Now, my question, Witness, I would like you to look at this intercept, the one on the right side, which is in your language. Can we minimise so that we get the full top part, the full header? Thank you. If you look at this intercept, the way it is there, and my colleague asked you a number of questions concerning information included in this intercept. Now, I suggest to you that if you just look at the intercept, and that is before you remember that on 19 January 1995 you were there. If I just look at this intercept I suggest to you that there is nothing on this intercept that – (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just didn't want -- just did want to point out that the -- what I see on my screen, anyway, refers to a different intercept. So I'm not sure if my colleague has noticed that or this is just a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm looking at it and I can't read it because it's too small, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You asked to have it minimised.

utterances.text: That would be on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Oh, yes, because it's a report that includes many intercepts. So if we can go on, the page number is 6615. Yes, this is the right page. And if we can move it up. Thank you.

utterances.text: Now, Witness, I refer your attention with that same question on the right side of your screen, and that is the intercept that starts with azimuth 110, and which would be a conversation between someone called Nikolic and someone called Popovic. Now, I repeat my question. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, I'm not so concentrated because the gentleman probably accidentally spoke of the location where I was, so I've lost my concentration because my identity is in question because I was the only one who was there from the beginning until the end, as a commander. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise to you, Witness, and we will go into closed session and if we can redact the information, Mr. President. We are looking at lines -- it's at page 60, lines 8 and 9, but it was also mentioned earlier.

utterances.text: 59, lines 12 and 13. 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: On page 13 [sic], indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, we need to redact lines 12 and 13. The second half of line 12 and all -- and the entire line 13 on page 59. And then on page 60, lines 8 and 9. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can go into private session for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I suggest to you that there is a possibility that this intercept actually involves a third person. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's also possible that maybe there's a mistake, and Mico is actually Nidjo. Is that another possibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: If you are implying that this might be a typo, an M instead of an N, I would not agree with you, and I apologise for that. Then there will be another typo in this letter "Ch."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Even if it's not a typo, it's simply that you typed the information that came from you, but it is the actual operator who listened to the conversation, he could have heard Mico when actually it was Nidjo. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: If the operator heard Mico, then he wrote Mico. And if you will allow me, I have an explanation for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: For example, my friend, and I'm not going to use my family name, refers to me by a shortened version of my family name, but this is my nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I understand this, Witness. But we have -- we already established that Mico is not the shortened version or the nickname of either Popovic, Pope, Nikolic, or Nidjo, and you acknowledged that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: The logic would say yes, but I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I understand, Witness. Now, if you look at where it says Mico, this line is attributed to N. And N, my understanding, would be Nikolic, based on this intercept, but I can hardly see Nikolic referring to himself and saying Nidjo. So if N was saying Mico, it means that there's actually someone else, called Mico, in that conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: If you are saying that there was a third person involved, then no. But it could be a third person that was referred to in the conversation. It is correct when you say that when Nikolic speaks he is not going to refer to himself as -- by this nickname. But there is a possibility that Mr. Popovic also has a nickname, and that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you don't know that either, and actually you cannot really assist the Court today with any of the contents of this intercept. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I believe that I have already answered that question. There could not have been a third person involved directly in that conversation. It is only possible that a third person was referred to in the conversation. I can only speculate that Mr. Popovic might have a nickname, but it's only speculation. I can't go into that, I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is exactly my point. This is speculation, and you cannot tell anything about exactly what is going on in that intercept, because what you did is you typed it and you had no involvement whatsoever in listening to the intercept. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: It is correct that I did not have headphones on my head, and that I was not sitting at the equipment. I was not involved in the transfer of the audio recording on to the paper. I've already said that a number of times here. But here, this person N, and the key word Mico, in the next line it is P, which means that the person called Popovic says, "Okay, go ahead. Tell me." These are the facts of this conversation. Look here, I apologise, maybe my words and my vocabulary is not as rich as yours but I'm trying hard. Here you have the person N using the key word Mico and the next word is, "Go on, say" uttered by P. So this person P, in -- understands this as person N addresses him. I don't know whether you understand me when I'm saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I understand, Witness, is that this is all speculation on your part and you don't know really what happened in that intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on. We've got enough on this, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question to you, Witness, is that you mentioned in response to a question which was posed to you by my colleague that whenever an intercept operator did not understand a word he would consult with his colleagues. Were you ever involved yourself in this guessing game, or the game of -- of helping another intercept operator in finding out what was heard on a tape? Were you ever yourself involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise. I would not call this a guessing game, and I apologise once again to you and to everybody here in the courtroom. War is no game for anybody. I apologise once again, and I would not accept your question in that particular form. I would not use the words guessing game. People behaved in keeping with the rules and this is no game. However, I believe I understood your question. Quite a number of times I would be called if the operator did not understand a word and I would try to help them, and there is no harm in that. They are my subordinates and I would be there to help them to try to understand what they couldn't understand. Would that be an answer to your question? Are you satisfied? With the proviso that I'm not happy with the term that you used, the guessing game.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise if I used word "guessing game" because my intention was to use the word that if an operator did not understand, he had to consult his colleagues. And my question was very simple, whether you were involved in finding out what the word that the intercept operator could not understand. My question to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has answer it. Let's move--

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you have answered that question. What I would like to know, is when you typed the conversation, any conversation, did you ever go back to the operator and say, "Listen, this conversation doesn't make sense. You must have heard wrong." Did you ever do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Look, nobody's perfect. We all speak in different ways, we use wrong cases, wrong tenses. We make mistakes when we speak, and when I read these, I can't be sure whether the person speaking made a mistake in their speech or what. There's no way for us to know whether it was the operator who made the mistake or whether it was the feature of the speech of the person who -- who spoke at the time. And you know that this happens. Nobody is perfect. And there is nobody in this world who has not used a word incorrectly. That's why we would listen to a conversation over and over again, if we had doubts about the accuracy of the transcript. And I apologise for taking up a lot of your time. For example, if I use a word incorrectly, then even my son will correct me and say, "You have used a wrong word." I'm trying to explain things to you. And I can answer that, yes, we did listen and relisten to the tapes, and I don't think that it is a mistake to listen to things over and over again. This is what I was trained to do when I was in the JNA, and we did that quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, I don't want to interrupt you and I thank you for this answer because that's exactly what I was trying to establish. And that was my last question, but I would just like to have a yes or a no. Once you had that piece of paper and you typed it, you typed whatever was on that piece of paper, and you did not go back to the operator. Can you please answer yes or no, if that is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Your Honours, my answer to the previous question and to the second question cannot be either yes or no. I would like to say that I did not check every piece of paper. However, if there was something illogical in that conversation or looked like a mistake or an error to me, then I would go and check that piece of paper with the operator. So I can't just answer by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, before we break, if you could give me the transcript page number in which you said that there is a reference to the second typist in addition to this witness who typed into computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was unable to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We need to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Kwon is only asking for the transcript line or page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. We will have a break now of 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon has finished. So the Borovcanin team, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We decided not to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Madam Fauveau for General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to clarify one thing with regard to the journal that you received from your colleague, and Your Honour, I think it might be best to be in private session for this series of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We can do that straight away. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that the unit to which you belonged also dealt with jamming of conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And within your unit there was a person who was specifically in charge of jamming, or were the operators who intercepted the conversations also in charge of jamming or scrambling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Not the operators who were in charge of interception. Not them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, there was a person who was specifically responsible for jamming conversations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Look, these conversations that we recorded from the RRU-1, and the RRU-800, we did not jam, because simply then we would be in the situation of jamming our source of information, but as part of the anti-electronic warfare activities of the 2nd Corps, there was a unit for anti-electronic activities. They were scramblers who did not only jam or disrupt enemy conversations, they also formed fake radio networks and spread misinformation so that the anti-electronic warfare of the other side would receive false, incorrect information and so on. That was a special, separate unit that, as part of the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit, that was doing that kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness Exhibit 5D198, and I'm sorry, I can't understand why though we introduced this exhibit into the system more than 48 hours ago, it still doesn't seem to be in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We found it, so I don't know what the problem is, but I'm sure Madam Usher will do her best. And, in fact, on the screen now, I do see the previous one on e-court. So it was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to request that exhibit not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that this report has to do with scrambling of conversations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that the one on the ELMO is the same one as we have in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's still the previous one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is that document, and I don't understand why it isn't in the system, because we did put it into the system more than 48 hours ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 198, 5D198. Let's proceed on the basis of the ELMO because we didn't find it either. Without broadcasting it, yeah. Thank you. Go ahead. Sorry, Madam Fauveau, for that interruption, but it was needed. The question to you, Witness, is, is it true that this report that you have next to you there on the ELMO deals with scrambling of conversations? And we haven't got your answer as yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This report states that I sent out information, and I was given the task of installing a mini Kobac device, which could operate in that range, and I submitted a report about what I did, and my conclusions. And it states here that all this was done in order to check whether jamming can be done, and I did that, and then five minutes later the signal on this frequency disappeared, which is normal, that the other side would protect its connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And is it true that the frequencies that you tried to jam during this trial that you were carrying out, were done with apparatus known as RRU-1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Sorry, but I think that earlier in my testimony today I have already said that we did not -- I mean, if my interpretation was correct, we were not catching the frequencies from the RRU-1. We did not have such a device to catch those frequencies. We were monitoring their RRU-1 connections.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It is surely my technical skills that are not sufficient, but what I would like to ask is whether the frequencies that you were trying to jam and this report deals with are, in fact, frequencies you were monitoring and recording with the help of an apparatus, RRU-1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes, with this frequency 258.275, 258 megahertz and 275 kilohertz, it means that that is the frequency within the range of an RRU radio relay device.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You were speaking earlier of the daily reports that you would send, namely on the condition of equipment and the equipment that you needed. Did you send those reports on a daily basis, once a day, or did you simply send them whenever it was necessary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Once a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in those daily reports, did you note down other information, all the relevant information relating to the important events of the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No. The reports that I sent out once a day, if we focus on reports on the operational state of the technical equipment, the devices, the antennas that we used in our work, those reports were sent once a day. But that sort of report is not the same as this kind of report. In the other reports there was a list of all the equipment, and then there was a column saying whether they were working properly or not, there were remarks relating to absences, if anyone was away due to illness, something like that. And then there were also remarks, what was needed in the coming period, so that when they came for the hand-over of duty, they could also prepare equipment, cables, food, medicines, and bring them. That kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau any time we don't need to stay in private session, please let us know. Oh, we are in open session. Okay, all right. We have reverted. Thank you. Go ahead. Sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in the daily reports, and I'm no longer referring at all to the report that you have before you, but in the daily reports that you would send, did you note down the frequencies on which you recorded conversations during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: I apologise, the reports on equipment, as far as I can remember, this is not where I recorded any frequencies. However, on the reports of the intercepted conversations on radio equipment, this is where I entered the workstation, the frequency and the equipment on which the conversations were recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And with regard to the jamming, were there specific reports on the frequencies that you tried to jam and those that you were able to jam? Or was this written down in your daily reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: No. I believe that we're talking at cross purposes here. The report, that I have in front of me, is an attempt to see whether this mini Kobac equipment can also do jamming. My department was not in charge of any jamming. This is just -- there was an order that I received to try and submit a report, based on which they could act. They could either purchase the equipment or transfer the whole thing to the jamming unit. This is just to provide an overview of the situation and see what results may be achieved. This was not a specific task that my department ever had.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you receive orders from your superiors, do you -- did you receive those orders by radio, by computer, or in printed form?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Well, you see, there were orders that I received through the Paket radio communication in this particular form, but there were also orders that I received on paper, as well as orders that I received verbally, but not via the Paket radio. But when we handed over our duty, when there was a shift change, then the commander would provide us with instructions, suggestions and orders as to how to proceed on a certain task. I preferred orders in written form, because they were best for me, although it was not always possible to issue written orders. But very often I received some instructions or guidance as to how to do things over the Paket radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... orders recorded in a logbook or some form of register when you received them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. Everything that was received through Paket radio, I believe that I've already told you that I had everything archived, everything that I received from my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And with regard to the orders that you had to give to your subordinates, did you print out those orders or did you communicate the information to them verbally only?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Verbally. We were all there in the same room. I don't know whether this suffices by way of explanation. We were in the same room, I would read the order out if I received it from the automatic data processing that collected information from everybody else, not only from us. And then they would be privy of some other information or they would know something we didn't know. They would suggest to us what we should do. Or for example, if they could not follow a frequency in a different location, then they would send us information or issue an order to us to see whether we can follow that frequency, what the signal quality and strength was, and then I would communicate that to my men. We would never communicate in writing, we would only communicate verbally from one desk to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness Exhibit P2437B but it might be better easier to give him the hard copy because I'd like him to look through all the pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the meantime, is it true you said in your statement that you would you write down your name on the reports that you would send? On page 2, paragraph 7, for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, would you please look at this report and tell me how come this report does not show your name anywhere?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It must not be broadcast, obviously, because there is the name of the site. Witness, please take the document in your hands, flip -- flip through it and see if you're in a position to answer Madam Fauveau's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our regular daily reports, this is where I put my signature. I did not sign these other reports because it was implied that I was the one who was sending them. And then those people at the automatic data processing would look at the date and they would know that the reports came from me. In the Paket radio communication, I had my signal code that changed every day and based on that code they would know that that report had arrived from my location.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What you have just said with regard to those reports containing the intercepted conversations, is it valid as well for -- it's valid as well for the other reports that you did sign. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-158
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, I'm not exactly clear on the question. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question, I'll rephrase it. If, as you say, the command knew your call sign and the code which changed on a daily basis, why was it necessary to sign some documents and not sign others? Because had you decided not to sign any of them, they would have deciphered the source of the information as being you in any case. I don't know if that made it clearer or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my regular reports on equipment, I always put my name. I really don't remember what the practice was in the other reports. And I really can't remember why I didn't sign these reports, these documents. I really can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean to stay on the question. Had you not signed those reports, would the command have identified you as the source of those reports? Or wouldn't they have been able to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command -- the command could identify everything based on my sign code. Let me go back to the Paket radio communication. I changed my sign code every day, the command did the same. We did it every day according to the plan of work, and this is something that is applicable to all -- all the military, everywhere in the world. And we also changed the code for the encryption of that particular report. If I were to put my own code, that was in the plan of work. And the command put a different code, then the encrypted signal could not have been decrypted. On the basis of that and on the basis of the code sign, they would immediately know where the report came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I take it that the Gvero and Pandurevic Defence teams do not wish to cross-examine the witness. Is that correct, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We have no question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, there is no re-examination. I'm not sure if I understood Mr. Haynes. Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Means --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was in the response to the question, "Is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, there is no re-examination at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Witness, we don't have any further questions for you. That means that your testimony finishes here, ends here. Our staff will assist you. On behalf of the Tribunal and my colleague, I would like to thank you for having come over and also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would offer -- well, first there is a pseudonym sheet, there is the intercept. Okay. Yes. We are offering the intercept. Because it's part of a report, I would ask that you would consider accepting it under seal. I know it would be marked for identification in any event. And that is identified as P02437A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness statement, I think I've previously referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections? We hear none. Of course the intercept --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are there any objections on the part of the Defence? Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. As far as P02946 document is concerned, that's the pseudonym sheet, we don't have any objections and we don't have any objections to the statement. But the supplement to this statement which belongs to another witness, this was not compiled by the witness that we heard today. And we are talking about shift duties for the month of January, 1995. We object to that because we believe that this document was not disclosed in a timely fashion, it does not bear the 65 ter number, and it was not the subject of the application for the submission of this document according to the Rule 65. Further on, the Defence intends to invite the owner of the notebook again. Today the entire notebook was disclosed, and that's why we intend to recall the witness and examine him on the contents of the notebook. If the witness had been examined on the notebook, then we could be talking about the criteria of relevance and reliability as well as the credibility of the document and its relevance for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have to leave it there because we have overstepped our time limit. We will take this up again tomorrow and finish because I suppose there are also documents that the Defence teams wish to tender and I wouldn't like to take more of the other Chamber's time. So we will come to this tomorrow morning. Thank you so much. Have a nice afternoon and evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
